ports.note: transport_default may be taken; a peer then binds an ephemeral port and advertises the real one through mDNS TXT/UDP announce/QR. discovery_udp must stay fixed because broadcast has no other way to be found.

discovery.note: Broadcast carries a fingerprint PREFIX only - of the certificate the socket actually serves. The full digest comes from GET /v1/hello's `served` and must match that prefix before pairing; a build too old to answer `served` has no separate leaf, so its `fingerprint` is the same number. Presence is not trust. A record without `fp` is not a candidate on any end - it is a name and an address with nothing to pin, and no end substitutes the address or the service name for it; where DNS-SD cannot carry TXT at all (Android below API 28, while this project's floor is 21) the whole mDNS channel is reported unavailable with that reason and the roster leans on the broadcast and the QR. A goodbye names the service, not the machine, and carries no `fp`: each end remembers which prefix that name last resolved to and withdraws only that channel's presence, so a peer still heard on the broadcast stays listed and one that was never remembered is left to the 15 s expiry - which is what actually removes a silent machine. The `port` of an announcement is the receiving port this end has open at the moment it sends: a machine that is not listening sends nothing and registers no mDNS service, because that number is what the listener gets dialled by. A published mDNS record is the same claim in the other channel, so it is re-asked on that beat rather than once when the discovery channel opens: withdrawn while nothing is listening, withdrawn and registered again when the port moved - a reader takes whichever path answered and a stale number here is the undialable machine spec §2 forbids. `ts` is when this end started listening, not when this packet left it, and no end reads it - each end measures the 15 s freshness on its own clock, against when it last heard that peer. The channels are not a feature switch: they come up with the listener and go down with it, and where one of them cannot start the UI names why and offers the QR. Hearing is not one of those halves: the mDNS browse and the 43721 receive socket do not close with the port, so any end can hear without being heard - the CLI's browse-only mode is the specimen. Tearing discovery down because this machine stopped receiving would make a person who only wants to send pay for a port they never needed. A person who turns them off by hand keeps that decision for the rest of the run.

tls.certificate: self-signed RSA-2048 leaf, CN=peer_id, 20 years - served by every end, because no platform TLS stack can present an Ed25519 leaf (Harmony #47, Android #106)
tls.trust: two digests per device: the RSA leaf's SPKI SHA-256 is what the socket is pinned to (QR `f=`, broadcast prefix, hello `served`), the Ed25519 identity key's is what pair signs and what the trust store keys on

transport.note: pair_code_static is spec §3: the code minted on first run stays until the user rotates it by hand, which is what lets the pairing QR be printed. The `p` of that string is the receiving port bound right now - the same answer spec §2 demands of an announcement - so the constant in ports.transport is never written into a pairing string, and an end with nothing open has no `p` to give and leaves the address and port out (PC raises, the phone's copied line carries neither). pair_code_ttl_s only bounds a build that ignores the flag. session_idle_timeout_s / offer_idle_timeout_s are floors, not timers: a receiver may reclaim later than they say, never sooner (spec §3, §4). pair_code_max_fails / pair_code_lock_s are spec §3's throttle and they are a SLIDING window: each failed attempt from one source lives 60 s on its own, so the block lifts 60 s after the OLDEST of the five, and an attempt refused while blocked adds no record of its own (it cannot extend the lock). The bucket is keyed by the peer's address on that socket and no end persists it across a restart. The three secrets a receiver keeps for the other side - the session token, the 6-digit code, the 8-char passphrase - come from each platform's cryptographic RNG (python `secrets`, `java.security.SecureRandom`, `cryptoFramework.createRandom`, `crypto.getRandomValues`), never from `Math.random()`; where 256 does not divide the alphabet the leftover bytes are thrown away instead of taken modulo. `peer_id`, offer/file ids and nonces are only required to be distinct, so no source is named for them. Pairing does NOT filter the source by address range: all three ends bind the wildcard address (PC `host=""`, Android `InetSocketAddress(port)`, Harmony `0.0.0.0`) and no pair path looks at the range its source address falls in. The LAN boundary lives in exactly one place in this repo - the installer's netsh rule `profile=any remoteip=LocalSubnet` - and only on a machine that ran that task; where the firewall prompt answered the first listen instead, the rule it leaves behind has a remote IP of *any* on the Public profile. Reachable scope is therefore a property of how a machine was installed, not of this protocol, and an address-scope check in a pair path would lock out loopback, port-forwarded and multi-homed setups, so the throttle counts tries and seconds only. Both optional pair keys are read by their *value*, not by key presence: `secret` absent or JSON null means 'this sender has no passphrase to offer' and `tls_fingerprint` absent, null or empty means 'the leaf I serve is the key that signed this', so a body carrying `"secret": null` pairs on the code alone on every end; an empty string is NOT absence - it is one wrong guess, refused with `BAD_PAIR_CODE {reason: "passphrase"}` and booked into that source's bucket, so a sender whose user left the passphrase blank must omit the key rather than send `""`. Shape is asked of a value a person typed or pasted before it goes on the wire, on both sides (PC `spec.code_reject`/`spec.pass_reject`, shared kernel `codeReject`/`passReject`, and the kernel's pairing-string parser asks both fields rather than one of them): a 7th digit or a lowercase letter is not a weaker promise, it is one of the `pair_code_max_fails` wrong guesses that lock this source out for `pair_code_lock_s` - so a sender that could never match says why locally and sends nothing. The one-session slot (spec §3) is given back by three named events on every end: the holder tapping 断开 (PC's device card and the settings 撤销, the phone's 断开 - which takes back BOTH halves, the peer this end dialled and the token handed to a peer that dialled in; a phone shows that button only for a peer it dialled out to, so a peer that only dialled in has to wait for one of the other two roads), the receiver restarting or its port being closed (PC's stop_listening drops the receiver object and the token map inside it; a phone's inbox outlives the listener, so 不再监听 releases those sessions by name), and the idle window running out, which also registers the loss: the reclaim says which peer it took back by fingerprint, never by a display string - a peer this device only ever dialled out to has no entry in the receiver's inbox, so its name there is a fallback built from the number, while the sender knows it under the name hello carried. A page deciding whether its own session went silent can only ask the number. Releasing a session is not revoking trust: the pin and the trust entry stay, so the peer released here returns with an empty pair code on its own signature alone. A dropped token is repaired by the sender, not by a person: a request that comes back `403 NOT_PAIRED` while this end still pins that key gets exactly one re-pair whose `code` is empty, and the promise is that this asks nothing of the user - no dialog, no typed code, and no transfer reported as a failure. The PC has three such call sites (`_call`, the offer poll, `_put_chunk`) because any of its requests can die there; the shared kernel has one because every request it makes goes through `authed()`. Whether a log line shows up is each end's own choice - §3 stopped promising the user sees nothing, because no end keeps that promise. The same call site is where the honest opposite lives: a peer that revoked the trust as well refuses the empty-code pair, and that has to reach the person as 需要配对码 rather than as a silent success. Both faces of that refusal answer with the same `BAD_PAIR_CODE` and nothing on the wire separates them, so the sentence is chosen from what this end knows: whether the `code` in that request was its own empty one. An empty code may only ask for a new pair code (nothing was typed, so 'enter it again' describes a typing that never happened); a code the person typed may only ask them to read the screen and enter it again (the key may be perfectly trusted, so 'no longer recognises this device' describes a revocation that never happened). Neither face is free: to a receiver that no longer knows the key an empty code is one wrong guess, so it is booked into that source's bucket like any other. PC `spec.pair_refusal(repair, proto)` with `PairNeeded` / `WrongPairCode` chosen by `send.py`, phone `cs-client.uts`'s `repairRefused(refused)`. The second layer (spec §3's passphrase) binds a sender that sends the field, not the wire: a stranger key that presents the correct code and omits `secret` pairs on every end and spends none of its source's five tries - that is the deliberate cost of the rule two sentences above ('absent or JSON null = a build with no passphrase concept'). Turning it into a gate would change the semantics of an existing field, and §7 demands a `protocol_version` bump for that, which would lock out those old builds, so v1 does not do it. A blank passphrase box is therefore loud on the sender side instead of silent: the PC's panel and its CLI each say the sentence, the phone writes it into 传输详情, and the sentence that says it is `spec.pass_omitted`. The throttle counts per source, so what stands in front of the 10^6 codes is 'five tries per `pair_code_lock_s` per machine', not a wall: N machines are N times the rate.

endpoints.purpose: version + capability probe; `fingerprint` names the identity key that will sign the pair request and `served` the certificate this socket presents (a scanner's prefix is checked against `served`); the optional chunk_pace_ms says how slowly a sender must write a body bigger than one TLS record (milliseconds per 4 KiB record, absent or 0 = as fast as you like) - a Harmony receiver needs 15, below that a 4 MiB chunk arrives whole with the wrong bytes and the receiving process can die on the attempt; `features` is this end's own capability list, sent verbatim as `transport.hello_features`, and it decides nothing in v1 (spec §7)
redeem a 6-digit code, pin the fingerprint
send a manifest, long-polls until the peer answers
which chunks are already on disk

BAD_PAIR_CODE.msgid: 配对码不正确或已过期

OFFER_UNKNOWN.msgid: 传输请求不存在或已结束

BAD_CHUNK_INDEX.msgid: 分块序号超出文件范围

PEER_BUSY.msgid: 对方正在处理另一个传输

relay.note: Cloud relay is built on the cloud-relay branch and must not fork this contract: the same seven endpoints are replayed through the relay, only the address resolution changes (peer_id -> relay session id).
